Yesterday, from 8:05 pm for about two and a half hours, a payment gateway fault meant **5,000 customers were charged but their payment failed**. Refunds were triggered automatically and reach customers within 7 business days (company policy).

brief.caption: Support dashboard at 9:30 am
rows: New tickets tagged "Money debited, order failed"
Open tickets from customers with more than one open ticket

items: 20 agents on today's shift, covering chat and email.
Each agent resolves about 45 tickets a day.
Two senior agents handle escalations. You report to the Head of Operations.

brief.text: The company and numbers are fictional, and every candidate gets a slightly different version. A calculator is fine.

reviewerGuide.text: Not scored. On the verification call, listen for the same voice and ask a related question to check it is the same person.
Capacity today is about 900 tickets (20 × 45) against 1,460 inbound plus 1,460 already open. More effort alone cannot catch up.
Strong answers go after demand:

items: 60% of new tickets are one issue with a known answer, so a proactive status message and a macro remove most of it.
37% of open tickets come from customers chasing an existing ticket, so merging duplicates shrinks the backlog immediately.

brief.text: You've just joined **Brewhaus Beans** as its first in-house performance marketer. Brewhaus Beans is a D2C coffee brand selling specialty coffee subscriptions online. The founder runs the business day to day, and an agency, BlueKite Digital, runs paid media.

brief.caption: Last month, as reported by each ad platform

brief.text: Same month, from the store backend

items: Average order value: **₹1,499**
Gross margin after product, shipping and payment costs: **50%**
About 19% of customers order again within 90 days.

brief.text: The company and numbers are fictional, and every candidate gets a slightly different version. A calculator is fine.

prompt.text: What is one marketing metric you think people rely on too much, and why?
Keep it under 45 seconds. This one is not scored; it just gets you talking.

reviewerGuide.text: Not scored. On the verification call, listen for the same voice and ask a related question to check it is the same person.

response.text: Swiggy's push notifications. They're written for the exact moment you're hungry and they're funny without trying too hard, so I actually read them.

prompt.text: It's your first morning at Brewhaus Beans. Looking at last month's numbers, **what worries you most, and what is the first number you would check before changing anything?**
Refer to specific figures. One sharp point beats a list of ten.

reviewerGuide.text: Strong answers notice at least one of these:

items: **Over-attribution.** Dashboards claim 4,595 orders, but the store recorded 3,304, so platforms over-claim by about 39%. Channel ROAS can't be taken at face value.
**Unit economics.** Blended CPA is ₹787 against a first-order break-even CPA of ₹750 (AOV × margin). The business is losing money on first orders, and repeat purchase (19%) has to carry the rest.
**Retargeting and brand search look too good.** 6.3x reported ROAS on retargeting mostly reflects people who were already going to buy.

reviewerGuide.text: Weak answers give generic advice ("refresh creatives", "optimise targeting") without touching the numbers, or take platform ROAS literally and pour budget into retargeting.

rubric.label: Works from the actual numbers
anchors: No specific figures; generic advice.
Quotes figures but does not connect them.
Connects two or more figures into a conclusion (e.g. CPA vs break-even).
Spots a non-obvious relationship, such as over-attribution, and quantifies it.

rubric.label: Measurement scepticism
anchors: Takes platform ROAS at face value.
Mentions attribution vaguely.
Says which channel numbers are least trustworthy and why.
Proposes a concrete check sized to this business (holdout, geo split, post-purchase survey, code/UTM audit).

rubric.label: Prioritisation
anchors: A list of everything.
Several priorities, unclear order.
One clear priority with a reason.
Clear priority plus what would change their mind.

response.text:
Biggest worry: the dashboards claim 4,595 orders but the store only saw 3,304, so about 39% of the credit is double-counted. That makes the 6.3x on retargeting close to meaningless.

First number I'd check: blended CPA (₹787) against what a first order is actually worth after margin (₹1,499 × 50% = ₹750). If blended CPA is above that we lose money on every first order, and the whole plan depends on the 19% who come back.

shown.title: The budget cut

choices.label: Spread the cut evenly across channels

prompt.text: The founder has cut next month's paid media budget by **20%**, to **₹20,80,000**, and wants orders to stay roughly flat. Retargeting is small; leave it out of this decision.
**Where does most of the cut come from?** Pick one, then explain:

items: why this channel,
what you expect to happen to store orders next month (give a number and how you got it),
the risk you are accepting, and the early warning you would watch.

lookingFor: Commits and reasons from unit economics

reviewerGuide.text: There is no single right answer. Good answers commit, estimate the order impact from marginal (not average) CPA, recognise that cutting prospecting starves retargeting and brand search later, and name an early-warning metric.
"Spread evenly" can be fine if it comes with a stated test plan; it is weak when it avoids the decision.

A number with no logic behind it.

A range with assumptions stated and a sense of confidence.

rubric.label: Risk and monitoring
anchors: Risk not mentioned.
Generic risk ("orders may drop").
Specific risk tied to the channel chosen.
Specific risk plus a metric, threshold and timing for reacting.

reviewerGuide.text: They chose **Spread the cut evenly across channels** in the previous question.

Tests whether they can admit the weakness and adapt. Strong: explains why even cuts hurt (campaigns fall below learning thresholds, fixed creative and agency costs), consolidates into the best marginal channels, and sets a clear test. Weak: defensive, or swings to an unreasoned all-in bet.

rubric.label: Updates on new information
anchors: Ignores or dismisses the new data.
Acknowledges it but keeps the plan unchanged without a reason.
Separates what the data shows from what it only suggests, and adjusts.
Adjusts in proportion to the evidence and says what would trigger a bigger change.

rubric.label: Explains the mechanism
anchors: No explanation of why it happened.
A plausible but generic explanation.

A correct mechanism plus how to prove it.

rubric.label: Concrete next step this week

reviewerGuide.text: Planted problems, roughly in order of how much they reveal:

items: **#2 Target ROAS is below break-even.** At 50% margin, first-order break-even ROAS is 2.00x, so a 1.7x target loses money on every attributed order, and more once you allow for platform over-claiming. The strongest expertise signal: generic AI critiques miss it unless given the margin.

**#5 The discount destroys margin.** A 20% discount cuts gross profit per order by about 40% (20% ÷ 50%), and the goal is flat volume, not growth.
**#1 Awareness spend won't pay back next month**, while the budget is being cut and orders must hold.

questions.question: In the YouTube example you shared from your past work, what was the actual budget size you moved, who had to sign off on it, and how did you prove those view-through conversions were cannibalizing existing demand?
questions.why: Tests genuine ownership and analytical rigor on a past project where her written answer lacked concrete budget numbers and methodology.
questions.listenFor: Specific budget figures and timelines, clear personal accountability for both the hypothesis and the rollback, and a concrete method used to measure cannibalization (such as baseline organic/brand search lift flattening).
questions.redFlags: Vague scale descriptions like 'a sizable chunk', deflecting ownership of the decision to others, or failing to explain how view-through attribution actually inflated numbers.

questions.question: You calculated that the agency's 1.4x ROAS target is below the 1.82x break-even floor. If the agency insists that 1.4x is necessary to acquire new customers at scale, how would you structure their targets so they don't lose money while testing?
questions.why: Probes her low ranking and fix scores on the agency critique to see if she can turn math critique into workable commercial direction.
questions.listenFor: Separating new customer acquisition targets from blended MER, setting hard budget caps on sub-break-even exploration, or requiring first-order contribution margin rather than platform ROAS reporting.
questions.redFlags: Backing down on the unit economics, dogmatically refusing any testing, or relying on vague buzzwords like 'better alignment' without tactical targets.

questions.question: You recommended setting up a two-week geo holdout on Meta to measure the halo effect on brand search. Walk me through the operational setup: how would you select the test regions and measure the lift?
questions.why: Checks whether her recommendation of a geo holdout was an offhand buzzword or a methodology she actually knows how to execute.
questions.listenFor: Selecting matched markets with similar historical baselines, isolating search/direct traffic by region, and defining clear pre/post lift metrics relative to control regions.
questions.redFlags: Suggesting a simple platform A/B split instead of a true geographic holdout, ignoring baseline differences between regions, or inability to explain how to measure brand search impact locally.

questions.question: When cutting ₹4,00,000 from Meta prospecting, you assumed marginal CPA would be 1.3 times the blended CPA, estimating roughly 415 lost orders. Walk me through the logic and arithmetic behind that 1.3 multiplier.
questions.why: Confirms whether her strongest analytical models reflect true understanding of diminishing returns or were just arbitrary estimates.
questions.listenFor: Clear explanation of diminishing marginal returns (the last spend is always less efficient than the first), and how trimming underperforming ad sets changes average efficiency to arrive at ~₹960 marginal CPA and ~415 orders.
questions.redFlags: Inability to recreate the arithmetic connecting ₹4,00,000, 1.3x CPA, and 415 orders, or stating it was merely an ungrounded guess.

questions.question: When reviewing the AI draft, you caught and removed an unrealistic claim that CAC would drop by 20%. If an executive had seen that draft first and expected that result, how would you walk them back to reality?
questions.why: Tests stakeholder management and the ability to defend disciplined, math-based expectations against unrealistic projections.
questions.listenFor: Using unit economics and platform saturation to explain why immediate 20% CAC drops are unrealistic, demonstrating calm confidence, and grounding expectations in total contribution profit.
questions.redFlags: Overpromising to placate the executive, blaming the tool without explaining the math, or avoiding difficult performance conversations.
